title.en: Grids: finding places on a map

text.en: Your friend says: meet me at the park. But on a big map, how will you tell exactly where? A grid of letters and numbers works like an address.

A map is divided into rows and columns by a grid. Columns are named with letters (A, B, C...) and rows with numbers (1, 2, 3...).
To locate a place, give the column letter first and then the row number, like C3.
On our sample map the school is at A1, the park at C3 and the well at E5.
To find a place: go along to the column letter, go down to the row number, and the square where they meet is the place.
Two places in the same row have the same number: A1 and E1. Places in the same column have the same letter: C1 and C3.
Always check which comes first on your map: here column letter, then row number.
(additional, not in the textbook) The same idea is used in chess boards, spreadsheets and the index of a road atlas.

problem.en: Which square is two columns to the right and two rows down from A1?

text.en: Moving two columns from A gives C.
Two rows down from 1 gives 3, so C3 - where the park is.

prompt.en: How do you describe a place on a grid map?

requiredIdeas.en: Say column letter then row number, like C3

commonMisconceptions.en: Swapping the order of letter and number

points.en: Grid maps use letters for columns and numbers for rows.
A location is given as letter then number, like C3.
Places in the same row share the number.
